items.excerpt: Chris Reid argues that humans will stop being the primary readers of published content, and that decades of structured-metadata work (FAIR principles) accidentally prepared publishers for machine readers. A direct challenge to how books and articles should be authored, structured and designed when the audience is an agent.

US textbook authors filed a class action against OpenAI alleging its models were trained on copyrighted educational material and now threaten to displace the textbook itself. The suit reframes AI harm from training to substitution of the authored work.

Maris Kreizman pushes back on the idea of an AI 'reading buddy' that smooths difficult prose into summaries, arguing that literary friction is the point. A craft-level argument about what AI reading assistants remove from the act of reading.

As AI systems retrieve texts across preprint servers, repositories and publisher sites, version ambiguity becomes a provenance problem. The piece argues persistent identifiers plus metadata must tell an AI which version of a work it actually read.

Reedsy co-founder Ricardo Fayet says keywords and search volume are dying as marketing metrics because readers now ask an AI what to read next — and Claude leans on Goodreads while ChatGPT and Gemini lean on Reddit. A concrete rework of how authors build discoverable 'internet footprint'.

Tech firms including Anthropic and Amazon are buying millions of physical books and guillotining their spines to scan pages as AI training data, with booksellers reporting bulk orders of rare, out-of-print titles through intermediaries.

An AI detection platform analyzing 2,000+ English-language paperbacks found 63% of religion titles on Amazon were likely AI-written, peaking at 78% for witchcraft books. A hard number on how far generated text has taken over a retail category.

Roundup flagging AI as the central topic across 200+ sessions at the IFLA World Library Congress in Korea, and China's Academy of Press and Publication preparing to unveil interim AI application standards for publishing at the Aug 27-29 Digital Publishing Expo.
Anthropic will watermark Claude-generated text and Substack is deploying Pangram detection, as author-verification tools proliferate. A survey of the emerging provenance layer around written work.

A new study found readers rated AI-generated stories higher than human-written ones when they believed a human wrote them, and writers are now deliberately roughening their prose — even adding typos — to avoid being mistaken for AI.

Editor Mary Kole says AI-generated manuscripts are 'clean, free of grammatical errors... and also soulless,' turning editing into uncredited authorship. She rewrote her contract with a 50% AI-assisted premium plus mandatory disclosure, and publishes the addendum.

Ashutosh Ghildiyal proposes a Cognitive Responsibility Framework splitting mechanical cognition (pattern work AI does well) from non-mechanical cognition requiring human judgment, warning of 'cognitive debt' when AI mediates engagement with evidence.

John Bond and Joanna Penn walk through where generative AI is actually used across publishing operations — including a book that ships AI-generated chapter summaries with usage guidelines — and Bond's claim that mainstream publishers experiment far more than they admit.

Friedman's industry roundup: EU transparency rules pushing embedded watermarks and signed provenance metadata into future models, a record five journalism award winners disclosing AI use, and HarperCollins' CEO calling for industry-wide AI solutions.

HarperCollins says AI will 'transform audiobooks' by expanding voices and sound effects and will drive overseas translation, while a record eight Pulitzer winners and finalists disclosed AI use and future entry forms will carry an AI disclosure question.
